1254.title: The call of the king
1254.hook: a good king's call, heard first, and then Christ's
1254.howItsDone: In an Ignatian retreat, the meditation on the call of the king is prayed before the second week begins, as a way of asking how fully the person wants to follow Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first week: sin, then mercy, then a colloquy at the foot of the cross. Your line was what have I done for Christ.

A recruiting speech, and an unusual one. A king stands before his people and says: come with me. You'll eat what I eat, wear what I wear, work with me by day and keep watch with me by night. Share the hard part, and you'll share the victory. Just: with me. Ignatius had been a soldier before his conversion, and this page of the Exercises sounds like it. He asks the person praying to hear that speech, and to notice how any decent person would answer. Then he turns the page.
screen: `COME WITH ME.` → `SAME FOOD, SAME WORK, SAME NIGHTS.` → `THEN HE TURNS THE PAGE.`

segments.voice: The call of the king stands at the doorway of the second week, and it works like a parable in two steps. First, a human king. Ignatius pictures a leader chosen by God, good and just, calling people in the terms of his own century to a hard campaign. The campaign isn't the point. The way he calls is. No orders from a safe distance. Same food, same clothes, same nights. Ignatius says it would be shameful to hear a call like that and hang back. Step two: if that's how we'd answer a good human leader, how much more Christ. Now the king is Christ our Lord, and the call goes out to every person. His aim, as Ignatius puts it, is to bring the whole world to his Father, and whoever wants to come must labor with him, so that following him in the pain, they may follow him in the glory. By the Sea of Galilee, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says to two fishermen: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men." Then Ignatius notices two kinds of answer. Anyone with judgment and reason, he says, will offer themselves for the work. Some will want to go further: to follow even into poverty and insult, if that is what Christ chooses for them. The Exercises leave that further offering to the person's freedom. And the meditation leaves a plain question about anyone who calls you: do they send you into the work, or walk into it first?
screen: `A KING WHO SHARES THE HARD PART.` · `HOW MUCH MORE CHRIST.` · `TWO KINDS OF ANSWER.` · `WHO WALKS INTO THE WORK FIRST?` · then, large: `COME YE AFTER ME.`

segments.voice: Hear the call in its shortest form: come after me. If you pray, answer Christ in your own words, or with today's line, I want to follow, and let one place for tomorrow come to mind: a kitchen, a desk. If you don't pray, think of someone you'd follow because they worked right beside you, and ask what made the difference.
The call of the king. A good king's call, heard first, so that Christ's call can be heard more clearly. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: I want to follow. Same food, same work, same nights. Same time tomorrow.

1255.title: Two standards
1255.hook: two banners: riches, honor, pride; and poverty, humiliation, humility
1255.howItsDone: In the second week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray the meditation on the two standards and end it with a triple colloquy to Mary, to Christ and to the Father, closing with the Hail Mary, the Anima Christi and the Our Father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the call of the king: a good king shares the hard part, and how much more Christ. Your line was I want to follow.

On a crowded field, a banner tells you where your side is standing. Lose sight of it and you can end up in the wrong company without ever deciding to. Ignatius takes that picture, from the world he knew as a soldier, and plants two banners in front of the person praying. Two flags, two leaders, two plans. The surprise is not that one is good and one is bad. Everyone expects that. The surprise is how small the first step is under each one.
screen: `A BANNER SHOWS WHERE YOUR SIDE IS.` → `TWO FLAGS, TWO LEADERS.` → `HOW SMALL THE FIRST STEP IS.`

segments.voice: A standard is a banner, the flag a company gathers under. Ignatius sets up two of them on two fields. On one, near Babylon, the enemy of our human nature sits on a throne of fire and smoke, frightening to look at, and sends his helpers into every town with a plan in three steps. First, riches. Then the honor that comes with them: being seen, being admired. Then, from honor, pride. And from pride, Ignatius says, the other vices follow. On the other field, near Jerusalem, Christ stands in a lowly place, beautiful and gracious, and sends his friends out with three steps of his own. First, poverty: poverty of spirit, and actual poverty if God chooses it for someone. Then a willingness to bear insult and being overlooked. From those comes humility, and from humility, the other virtues. Nobody leaps into pride. It starts with wanting a little more, then wanting to be noticed for having it. And Christ's first step is just as small: holding things lightly, the indifference from three days ago. Jesus says it plainly in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "No man can serve two masters." The meditation ends with three conversations, asking Our Lady, then the Son, then the Father for the grace to be received under Christ's standard, each closed with a prayer the Church already knows: a Hail Mary, the Soul of Christ, an Our Father.
screen: `A STANDARD IS A BANNER.` · `RICHES, THEN HONOR, THEN PRIDE.` · `POVERTY, THEN INSULT, THEN HUMILITY.` · `THE FIRST STEP IS SMALL.` · then, large: `NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.`

segments.voice: Walk back through the last day or two and notice, without scolding yourself, the tug of a first step: wanting a little more, wanting to be seen, needing to be right. Then look for one moment that leaned the other way, like letting someone else take the credit. If you pray, ask, as the Exercises do, for the grace to be received under Christ's standard.
Two standards. Two banners on two fields, each with a plan in three small steps: riches, honor, pride; or poverty, insult, humility. Today's word.
Your line: under his standard. The first banner rarely looks evil; it can look like a nicer car. See you tomorrow.

1256.title: Three kinds of people
1256.hook: three ways people deal with an attachment
1256.howItsDone: In the second week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray the meditation on the three classes of people after the two standards, using it to test how free they are before making a choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two standards: riches, honor, pride, or poverty, insult, humility, each starting small. Your line was under his standard.

Three people have each come into a large sum of money. Not stolen. Not quite clean either: they got it, Ignatius says, not purely for the love of God. And now each one feels the weight of it. Not the money itself, the grip it has on them. All three want to be at peace with God and rid of that grip. They even agree on the goal. What separates them is what they actually do next. Ignatius sets them side by side in the second week and lets the one praying watch.
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, ONE FORTUNE EACH.` → `THE WEIGHT IS THE GRIP.` → `SAME GOAL, THREE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The first person wants to be free of the attachment. Really wants it. But never takes the means. Next month. After this busy stretch. Ignatius says they put it off right up to the hour of death. The second person also wants to be free, but on one condition: keeping the money. They'd like God to come around to what they've already decided. They'll pray about it, as long as the answer is yes. The third person wants to be free in a different way. They don't cling to keeping it, and they don't cling to giving it up. They want to keep it or let it go only as God moves them and as serves God better. And while they wait to see which, they live as if they'd already let it go in their heart. That person might keep the money. The meditation isn't about the money. It's about who holds whom. Jesus puts it in one line, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Ignatius adds an honest note: if you feel a pull against letting go, ask in prayer for exactly the thing you resist, even against your own inclination. He doesn't pretend the third way is easy. The meditation ends with the same three conversations as yesterday's. And it isn't only about money: a phone, a grudge, a role at work that has become who you are.
screen: `THE FIRST: SOMEDAY.` · `THE SECOND: ONLY IF I KEEP IT.` · `THE THIRD: AS GOD MOVES ME.` · `WHO HOLDS WHOM?` · then, large: `WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one attachment, something you own, a role, a habit, a plan you've already settled, and ask honestly which of the three you are with it: someday, bargaining, or free. No grade. For this sit, try the third way: hold it with an open hand, neither clutching it nor throwing it away. If you pray, ask God to move you whichever way serves.
Three kinds of people. One puts it off, one bargains, and one wants only what serves God, keep it or not. Today's word.
Your line: really free. One says someday, one bargains, one opens the hand and waits. Rest well.

1257.title: Rules for discernment
1257.hook: learning to read the movements of the heart
1257.howItsDone: People who pray in the Ignatian way use the rules for discernment of spirits throughout a retreat and in daily life, often talking over their consolations and desolations with a spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three kinds of people: one puts it off, one bargains, one wants only what serves God. Your line was really free.

A wounded soldier is stuck in bed, bored, in a house with the wrong books: no adventure stories, only a life of Christ and lives of the saints. So he alternates. For hours he daydreams about a great lady and glorious deeds. Then he reads, and daydreams about doing what the saints did. Both daydreams are pleasant while they last. But afterward, as Ignatius tells it later, he notices something odd. The knightly dreams leave him dry and unsatisfied. The saintly ones leave him content, long after the book is closed. He starts paying attention to the aftertaste.
screen: `A SOLDIER IN BED, WITH THE WRONG BOOKS.` → `TWO KINDS OF DAYDREAM.` → `HE NOTICES THE AFTERTASTE.`

segments.voice: Back on day two hundred thirty-eight you met consolation and desolation; here are the rules behind them. In everyday speech, discernment means sound judgment. Ignatius means something narrower. His Rules for the Discernment of Spirits are about the movements inside a person: the pulls, moods and thoughts that come and go. Consolation is any movement that draws a person toward God: more faith, hope and love, a quiet peace, even tears. Desolation is the reverse: darkness, restlessness, a drag toward low things, feeling far from God. The subtle part: the same feeling can mean opposite things, depending on which way a person is heading. For someone drifting away from God, the enemy offers easy pleasures, and the good spirit stings the conscience. For someone growing toward God, it flips: the enemy stings and discourages, and the good spirit gives courage and peace. So a feeling isn't a verdict. It's a signal, read in context. The First Letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "believe not every spirit, but try the spirits if they be of God." One plain rule: in a time of desolation, make no change. Stay with what you decided in a clearer hour. And in consolation, store up strength for the next dark stretch. The enemy, he adds, wants secrets kept, and loses power once things are told to a wise confessor or guide. And if a dark stretch ever turns into not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `CONSOLATION AND DESOLATION.` · `THE SAME FEELING, TWO MEANINGS.` · `IN DESOLATION, MAKE NO CHANGE.` · `TELL IT TO A WISE GUIDE.` · then, large: `TRY THE SPIRITS IF THEY BE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Let today replay quickly, like flipping through photos on a phone, and stop at one moment that left a good aftertaste, then at one that left you dry or restless. Just name them, this drew me toward, this pulled me away, without analyzing. If you pray, bring both to God and ask for light to read them.
Discernment. For Ignatius, learning to read the movements of the heart, consolation and desolation, and where each one leads. Today's word.
Your line: read the heart. It began with a soldier noticing an aftertaste. I'll be here tomorrow.

1258.title: The deathbed test
1258.hook: Ignatius suggests weighing your choice from your deathbed
1258.howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats and in spiritual direction, people facing a major decision in a calm time are invited to use Ignatius's tests, including advising a stranger and considering the choice as if at the point of death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rules for discernment: consolation, desolation, and making no change in the dark. Your line was read the heart.

There's a decision on the table. A job, a move, a yes or a no to someone. The list of pros and cons has been written twice, and it comes out even. Nothing inside is pulling hard either way. Ignatius has a tool for exactly this moment. Stop looking at the choice from where you're standing now, he says. Look at it from the very end of your life, from the bed you'll die in. It sounds grim. Some people find it oddly calming.
screen: `THE LIST COMES OUT EVEN.` → `NOTHING IS PULLING.` → `LOOK FROM THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: The deathbed test sits in the part of the Exercises about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He describes three times when a person might choose. Sometimes God moves the will so clearly there's no doubting it. Sometimes the choice becomes clear through yesterday's movements, consolation and desolation. And sometimes it's a calm time, nothing stirring, and a person has to use their reason. For that calm time he offers a few tests. First, think of someone you've never met, whom you wish every good, and ask what you'd advise them. Then follow your own advice. Second, today's test: consider, as if at the point of death, what you would then wish you had decided, and decide that way now. Third, picture yourself before God at the judgment and ask the same question. The hope is that much of what pulls at a decision, what people will think, what's comfortable this year, goes quiet at the end, and what's left is simple. Did I love? Did I serve? Was I honest? Ecclesiasticus, in the Douay-Rheims, puts it plainly: "In all thy works remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin." This isn't meant to be morbid. Ignatius sets it right beside the stranger test, which is gentle and practical, and both lift you out of the middle of the moment. If thinking about the end ever stirs thoughts of wanting to die, set this test aside and reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or local emergency help.
screen: `AN ELECTION IS A CHOICE.` · `A CALM TIME NEEDS REASON.` · `ADVISE A STRANGER, THEN LISTEN.` · `WHAT WOULD I WISH, AT THE END?` · then, large: `REMEMBER THY LAST END.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice in front of you, big or small, and let the two options sit side by side. Let time run forward, gently, to the end of a long life, and look back at this choice from there: which way do you wish you had gone? Then come back to today, to the chair you're sitting in; if you pray, ask for the courage to choose from there.
The deathbed test. Weighing a choice from the end of life, and deciding now the way you would wish you had then. Today's word.
Your line: from the end. The end of a long life is a steadier place to stand. See you tomorrow.

1259.title: The third week
1259.hook: walking with Christ through the passion
1259.howItsDone: In the third week of an Ignatian retreat, people contemplate the passion scene by scene, from the Last Supper to the burial, asking for the grace of sorrow with Christ in his sorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the deathbed test: weigh a choice from the very end, and decide now as you'd wish you had then. Your line was from the end.

It's late, in a garden on the Mount of Olives. The supper is over. Jesus takes three of his friends a little way apart and asks them for one thing. Not to argue his case. Not to fight. Not to find a way out. Just to stay awake and stay near. Then he goes a short distance further, falls on his face, and prays. When he comes back, they're asleep. The third week of the Spiritual Exercises begins on nights like this one, and asks the person praying to do what those friends could not.
screen: `A GARDEN, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `JUST STAY NEAR.` → `THEY FELL ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: The third week walks with Christ through the passion: from the supper, through the garden, the arrest, the trials, the cross and the tomb. What's striking is what Ignatius asks the person to want. Not insight. Not a lesson. Sorrow with Christ in sorrow, anguish with Christ in anguish. With is the word that matters. The first week looked at sin, and could feel like standing in the dock. This is companionship: staying beside someone who is suffering. Ignatius gives a few things to notice. What Christ suffers in his humanity. How the divinity hides itself: he could stop it, and doesn't. And that he suffers this for me, and what I ought to do and to bear for him. He even suggests a fast for the imagination: during this week, don't call up joyful thoughts, even good and holy ones like the resurrection. Don't skip ahead to Sunday. In the garden, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says to his three friends: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." He didn't ask them to fix anything. And the Gospel is honest: they slept, more than once. The third week gives the one praying a second chance at that night. Sometimes nobody can make the pain stop. Staying is still something. And if the pain is your own and feels like too much, you don't have to stay in it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `FROM THE SUPPER TO THE TOMB.` · `SORROW WITH CHRIST IN SORROW.` · `THE DIVINITY HIDES ITSELF.` · `DON'T SKIP AHEAD TO SUNDAY.` · then, large: `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Choose one scene, the garden at night, the road with the cross, or the foot of the cross, and put yourself there quietly, a few steps behind, noticing the faces, the dust, the sounds. Don't try to say anything clever; just stay. If you pray, ask, as Ignatius does, for sorrow with Christ in his sorrow; if you don't, keep someone who is suffering company in your thoughts.
The third week. Walking with Christ through the passion, from the supper to the tomb, asking to stay beside him in his sorrow. Today's word.
Your line: suffer with. He asked his friends only to stay. Go gently.

1260.title: The fourth week
1260.howItsDone: In the fourth week of an Ignatian retreat, people contemplate the appearances of the risen Christ, asking for the grace to rejoice in his joy and noticing how he consoles each person he meets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third week: walking with Christ through the passion, and staying near. Your line was suffer with.

A woman is crying outside a tomb in the early morning. The body she came to care for is gone. Someone is standing behind her, and she takes him for the gardener. She asks him, if he has carried the body away, to tell her where. He doesn't give her a speech about the resurrection. He doesn't show her proof. He says one word, and it's her name. That's enough. The fourth week of the Exercises is full of moments like this, and Ignatius has a title for what Christ is doing in each.
screen: `CRYING OUTSIDE A TOMB.` → `SHE TAKES HIM FOR THE GARDENER.` → `HE SAYS HER NAME.`

segments.voice: The fourth week turns from the tomb to the risen Christ. Yesterday, the divinity hid itself in the passion. Now, Ignatius says, it shows itself, in the resurrection and in what it does. He asks the one praying to watch for one thing in every appearance: the office of consoler. Office, as in a job. Christ carries out the work of consoling, and Ignatius says to compare it with the way friends console one another. Mary Magdalene at the tomb, in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus saith to her: Mary. She turning, saith to him: Rabboni." Two disciples on the road to Emmaus, sad and confused, and he walks beside them, talking, a long way before they know who he is. Peter, who had denied him, is given breakfast on the beach. Each is consoled in a way that fits them. Ignatius begins the week somewhere surprising: with an appearance to Our Lady, his mother. He admits scripture doesn't mention it, and says it should be understood all the same, since scripture tells of him appearing to so many others. The grace to ask for changes too: not sorrow now, but to be glad and rejoice in Christ's joy. His joy, not only mine. Even the outward helps change: in this week Ignatius suggests light, fresh air, and thinking of things that bring joy.
screen: `THE HIDDEN DIVINITY SHOWS ITSELF.` · `THE OFFICE OF CONSOLER.` · `A NAME, A WALK, A BREAKFAST.` · `REJOICE IN HIS JOY.` · then, large: `MARY. RABBONI.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last week for one moment of consolation, in Ignatius's sense: a kind word, a sky, a laugh you didn't expect, a peace that came out of nowhere. Let it play again, notice who brought it or how it arrived, and stay with the gladness without hurrying past. If you pray, thank Christ for it; if you don't, let the good of it land.

The fourth week. The risen Christ as consoler, meeting each person in the way that fits them. This week ran from the call of the king, through the two standards and the art of choosing, to the passion and the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: the consoler. Not with arguments: with a name, a walk, a meal. That's today, done.
